section_title: Responses to halt land degradation and to restore degraded land
summary: This chapter evaluates responses to land degradation and restoration, categorizing them into enabling/instrumental and direct biophysical/technical responses. It emphasizes that there is no one-size-fits-all solution and that effectiveness depends on local context, drivers, and the integration of indigenous and local knowledge.

passages.text: The most cost-effective approach to reduce land degradation in the long run is to follow the adage “prevention is better than cure” (well established).

Agroecology, conservation agriculture, agroforestry and sustainable forest management can successfully avoid land degradation, while enhancing the provision of a range of ecosystem services (well established).

Conservation agriculture, agroecology, agroforestry and traditional practices are effective ways to use and manage soil and land resources sustainably (well established). These management practices can be effective in reducing soil loss and improving soil quality, as well as other biogeochemical functions and processes in soils including: biological productivity; hydrological processes; filtering; buffering and nutrient cycling; and habitat quality for soil and above-ground organisms and communities.

heading_path: 6.3 DIRECT BIOPHYSICAL AND TECHNICAL RESPONSES TO LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION
passages.text: Cropland soil degradation is very site specific and can occur physically, chemically and/or biologically. Potential responses to degradation include using: (i) a landscape approach; (ii) conservation agriculture; (iii) integrated crop, livestock and forestry systems; (iv) agroforestry; (v) enhanced plant genetics; and (vi) integrated watershed management.

heading_path: 6.3 DIRECT BIOPHYSICAL AND TECHNICAL RESPONSES TO LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION
passages.text: Conservation agriculture, as defined by the FAO, is characterized by three specific actions including: (i) continuous minimum mechanical soil disturbance; (ii) permanent organic soil cover; and (iii) diversification of crop species grown in sequences and/or associations.

heading_path: 6.3 DIRECT BIOPHYSICAL AND TECHNICAL RESPONSES TO LAND DEGRADATION AND RESTORATION
Integrated crop, livestock and forestry systems
passages.text: Another strategy for restoring degraded cropland (sometimes referred to as sustainable intensification) is to incorporate perennials and cattle into traditional row-crop production systems. These systems not only increased food and feed production at farm and regional levels, but also improved many ecosystem services.
